name: Karl Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me, Karl. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party, and nothing you say gets your name attached. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm the senior copywriter and campaign lead at Field & Oat, which makes oat milk and oat yoghurt, and our office is above a bike shop near the canal. Most mornings start with a brief from Helen, our head of brand, then I'm writing: carton copy, posters, the odd radio script. I still sketch every campaign idea in a paper notebook before I touch a laptop.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the moment a line clicks, when six words on a carton make someone smile at the supermarket shelf. What wears me out is the meetings about the meetings, and lately the constant push to try AI writing tools. Helen sends links every week and I just don't open them. I'm 27 and I already sound like my grandad, I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, honestly, and probably a bit too loudly at the Friday drinks. Online I'd write something about how good copy was never just words in the right order. I'd be kind about it though, because plenty of people were scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be relieved, but not completely. Helen would still want the boring stuff, like product listings for the online shops, done by software, and that's a chunk of what Dario, my junior, does. And our rent went up again in September, so even the plain normal world has its squeeze.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do, and I'd keep refusing the tools for my own writing. I'd push to get Dario moved onto proper campaign work so he isn't the one squeezed out. I'd also join the creative workers' union properly, not just read their newsletter, because the next push will come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, with a small itch. The itch is that the company will still look at the copy budget and wonder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned rent. What does the money side look like for you and your partner right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lena, my partner, teaches at a primary school, so between us we're fine but not comfortable. We've got about four months of savings, and a chunk of that is meant to be a deposit one day. If my pay stood still for two years while rent kept climbing, the deposit would just stay a dream.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd refuse the tools even in this world. What if Helen made it part of your review?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If my boss Helen made AI tools part of my review, I'd write the best campaign of the year by hand and dare her to mark me down. I'm stubborn, but I'm good, and she knows it. I think she'd back off.

say: I'd say **good copy** was never just words in the right order.
I'd be **kind** about it, because plenty of people were scared for nothing.
think: I'm **relieved**, but the boring writing still drifts to software.
My junior **Dario** does those product listings, so he's the one squeezed.
Rising **rent** means even a normal world is tight for us.
do: Keep **refusing** AI tools for my own campaign writing.
Push Helen to move **Dario** onto proper campaign work this spring.
Join the **creative workers' union** as a paying member, not just a reader.
feel: Mostly **calm**, with a small itch about the **copy budget**.
S0.quote: If my boss Helen made AI tools part of my review, I'd write the best campaign of the year by hand and dare her to mark me down.
fieldNote: Karl is **proud of craft** and treats refusing AI as a matter of principle, not ignorance.
His real worry here is **Dario**, the junior whose routine work software takes first.
Rent and a **stalled deposit** keep him from calling this world fully safe.

steps.text: Keep writing every Field & Oat campaign by hand, no AI
Sign up as a paying member of the creative workers' union

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a choice companies are making, not the weather. At work I'd ask out loud who decided that copy is just a cost. Online I'd share every story of a team that got cut so a dashboard looks nicer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm in trouble in this one. Writing is the first thing on the card, and I'm the person who never learned the tools. Being among the best only helps if the people deciding can tell good copy from fine copy, and most of them can't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finally sit down and learn the tools, slowly and grudgingly, maybe a weekend course in January. I'd go hard on the union: getting Field & Oat's creative team to ask for a say in how the tools are used. And I'd stop eating lunch out, and put the deposit savings aside as an emergency fund instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in the chest. Like being told the skill you're proudest of is the one that's cheapest now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Field & Oat would you worry about first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dario, for sure, and Mira on social media, because their work is exactly what the tools spit out in seconds. I'd be okay for a year or two because I run campaigns, not just lines. But a team of five becomes three, and I'm not sure I'm one of the three if Helen wants someone who loves the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lena the evening the first person on your team is let go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner Lena that being good at your job is a lot less useful when the people deciding can't tell good from good enough. Then I'd probably go quiet and wash every dish in the flat. She knows that's my tell.

say: I'd say cutting copywriters is a **company choice**, not the weather.
I'd share stories of **teams cut** just to make a dashboard look nicer.
think: **Writing** is first on the list, and I never learned the tools.
Being **among the best** only counts if bosses can spot the difference.
A team of **five becomes three**, and I might not be kept.
do: Take a **weekend course** on AI writing tools in January, reluctantly.
Push the creative team to ask for a **say** in tool use.
Turn the **deposit savings** into an emergency fund and stop lunches out.
feel: **Tight** in the chest, like my **proudest skill** is suddenly the cheapest.
S1.quote: I'd tell my partner Lena that being good at your job is a lot less useful when the people deciding can't tell good from good enough.
fieldNote: Karl moves from principle to **grudging learning** once his own team is cut.
He blames **company choices**, not the technology, and turns to the union first.
He openly doubts he'd be one of the **three kept** from five.

steps.text: Book a weekend course on AI writing tools in January
Organise Field & Oat's creative team to ask for a say on tools
Move the house deposit fund into an emergency account
Bring lunch from home instead of buying it near the canal

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd be angry, and I'd say it plainly: nobody voted for this. I'd be at the first rally, and I'd post about a pause and a tax on whoever profits. At work I'd say we should all stick together and refuse to train our replacements.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, in two years my job is gone, full stop. My job is almost all thinking work, screens and words and pitches, so I get hit on day one, not in 2031 when the robots come. I'd have maybe four months of money and a skill nobody is paying for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd stop pretending and look at hands-on work, because that gives me three more years. My uncle Bilal, my mum's brother, fits kitchens and he's offered me work before, so I'd ask him seriously. I'd keep my job as long as they'd have me, cut everything else, and spend weekends with the union on whatever campaign is pushing for income support.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, mostly. And a bit ashamed that I spent two years refusing to even look.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said hands-on work buys you three more years. How do you feel about trading copy for kitchens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a step back and a lifeboat at the same time. I'm 27 and I've got a master's degree, and I'd be learning to level cabinets from a man who calls my job colouring in. But three years of wages is three years, and I'd rather earn them than wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the plans you and Lena had, the deposit and the rest?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The deposit would be dead, and we'd probably move somewhere cheaper, maybe nearer Lena's school. Teachers might last a bit longer, since kids still need a grown-up in the room. I'd be leaning on her, which I hate saying.

say: I'd say **nobody voted** for this and call for a pause.
I'd tell colleagues to stick together and **refuse to train** our replacements.
think: My work is almost all **thinking work**, so it goes on day one.
I'd have about **four months** of money and an unpaid skill.
**Hands-on** work only buys about three extra years.
do: Ask **Uncle Bilal** for kitchen-fitting work within the first months.
Cut spending to **essentials** while keeping the copy job as long as possible.
Spend weekends campaigning with the union for **income support**.
feel: **Sick**, and a bit **ashamed** I spent two years refusing to look.
S2.quote: My job is almost all thinking work, screens and words and pitches, so I get hit on day one, not in 2031 when the robots come.
fieldNote: Karl sees clearly that **desk work** has no three-year buffer.
He reaches for **family**, Uncle Bilal's kitchen business, as a lifeboat.
His regret about **refusing the tools** surfaces here for the first time.

steps.text: Ask Uncle Bilal for paid kitchen-fitting work within three months
Cut spending to rent, food and travel only
Campaign at weekends with the union for income support
Put the house deposit plan with Lena on hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have five years and we're wasting them. At work I'd push for the company to commit to retraining every one of us, in writing. Online I'd be the annoying person posting about union contracts every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough to see it and not enough to dodge it. I'd be 32 when AGI lands and 35 when robots come, so I'd have to pick a second life fast. Being stubborn doesn't work when the clock is that visible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the AI tools properly in the first year, so I could stay useful at Field & Oat for three or four of those five years. I'd start an evening course in something hands-on, probably carpentry, since Uncle Bilal's work makes sense to me now. And I'd save hard, trying to get from four months to a full year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like a slow countdown. Less panic than the two-year one, more dread.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years gives you time. Why does it still sound so dark to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because my whole field goes either way, it just goes politely. The extra time lets me land somewhere, but the somewhere is still not writing. I chose this work because I loved words, and none of the five years brings that back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame, if anyone, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I blame the handful of firms building this and the governments letting them run. Not Helen, not the brand, they're just in the river like me. With five years' warning my whole field still goes, it just goes politely.

say: I'd say we have **five years** and we're wasting them.
I'd push Field & Oat to promise **retraining** for every one of us, in writing.
think: I'd be **32** at AGI and 35 when robots come.
**Stubbornness** stops working when the clock is that visible.
The extra time helps me land, but **not in writing**.
do: Learn the **AI tools** properly in year one to stay useful longer.
Start an evening **carpentry course** to follow Uncle Bilal's trade.
Save hard to grow from four months to **a year** of cushion.
feel: Like a **slow countdown**, less panic but more **dread**.
S3.quote: With five years' warning my whole field still goes, it just goes politely.
fieldNote: The extra time turns Karl from refusing to **learning tools** as a bridge.
He plans a **two-step exit**: stay useful, then move to carpentry.
He grieves the loss of **writing** itself, not just income.

steps.text: Learn the AI writing tools properly in the first year
Enrol in an evening carpentry course at the local college
Save until the cushion covers a full year
Push Field & Oat to sign a written retraining promise

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if we use it, and I'd want laws, retraining money and a share of the profits sorted early. At work I'd be the one asking about it in every all-hands meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years changes a lot for me. I'd be 37, which is still young enough to have a whole second career. I could even have another eight good years as a copywriter before it bites.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep writing, but I'd start learning the tools at my own pace this year, which I've avoided. I'd take a part-time course in teaching, because Lena loves it and kids still need people. And I'd keep putting money aside every month, bit by bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. Still uneasy underneath, but it feels like a problem with a shape.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've moved from carpentry to teaching. What changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years I don't need the fastest lifeboat, I can pick one I'd actually like. Teaching keeps me close to words and stories. Carpentry was about survival.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And would the ten years change anything at home, for you and Lena?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd keep the deposit plan alive, maybe buy a small place in four or five years. Lena would say having a teacher's income and a future teacher's income is boring and safe. Boring and safe sounds lovely right now.

say: I'd say **ten years** is a gift if we use it well.
I'd ask about **retraining money** and profit-sharing in every all-hands.
think: At **37** I'd still be young enough for a second career.
I might get **eight more years** as a copywriter first.
do: Learn AI tools **at my own pace** starting this year.
Take a **part-time teaching** course over the next two years.
Put a little **money aside** every month.
feel: **Calmer**, but still **uneasy** underneath, like a problem with a shape.
S4.quote: With ten years I don't need the fastest lifeboat, I can pick one I'd actually like.
fieldNote: Time lets Karl choose by **preference**, not survival: teaching over carpentry.
Even here he expects his **copy job** to end, so the worry stays.
Ten years makes room for **family plans** he'd otherwise drop.

steps.text: Start a part-time teacher training course within two years
Try one AI writing tool a month at Field & Oat
Move a fixed sum into savings every payday
Keep saving the house deposit with Lena

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily, because my work is screens and words and I'd have no time at all. What would help is real income support while people retrain, paid for by the firms making the money, and a union with enough weight to bargain over how this lands. Cheap evening courses in trades and teaching would help too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what I'd miss. I'd miss the notebook, the bad first ideas and the good tenth one. Nobody counts that as a loss, but it's the reason I do the job at all.

headlineQuote: I'd miss the notebook, the bad first ideas and the good tenth one.
portrait: Karl is a **27-year-old** senior copywriter at Field & Oat, an oat-drinks brand, who writes by hand first.
He is **progressive** and pro-union, and blames AI firms and governments rather than his boss.
He has **refused AI tools** on principle and later regrets that in the faster scenarios.
With **four months** saved and rising rent, he sees his desk job as first in line.
His escape routes shift with time: **kitchen fitting** at two years, carpentry at five, teaching at ten.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his screen-and-words job would vanish with no time to prepare.
whatWouldHelp: **Income support** while retraining, paid by the firms profiting, and a stronger **union** to bargain.
